newsitem.title: FRANCE: French call money easing boosts hopes for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: French call money easing boosts hopes for rate cut.

text.p: A cut on Monday in French call money, a semi-official interest rate, bolstered hopes that the intervention rate will be cut when the Bank of France's monetary policy council meets on October 31, economists said.

The overnight rate, closely steered by the Bank of France, eased 1/16 of a percentage point to 3-1/4 3/8 percent on Monday, the third cut in call money since the last intervention rate cut on September 19.
"They're at the point where they have to consider cutting the intervention rate," said Philippe Brossard, head of reserach at ABN Amro in Paris.

Economists said the proximity of the overnight rate to the intervention rate, which sets the floor for French money market rates, meant the intervention rate would be cut soon while the recent strength of the franc provided a favourable backdrop.

"The spread between (call money) and the floor rate is now only six basis points, a signal that the intervention rate will be cut sometime," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris. "I still favour the end of October monetary policy council meeting as a likely date for a 10 basis point cut."
Brossard also said a 10 basis point cut in the intervention rate to 3.15 percent on October 31 was a possibility, even if the Bundesbank were to leave its key repo rate unchanged at 3.00 percent.
The Bank of France "won't want to be in a hurry but there's still a possibility they'll cut even if the Bundesbank doesn't do anything on Thursday," he said.

The gap between the French intervention rate and the German repo rate is currently 25 basis points. Although economists expect this gap to narrow steadily in the run up to European economic and monetary union, most expect the Bank of France to preserve some difference for now.

"Ultimately the Bank of France can cut the rate much, much closer to Germany," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais. He said he expected the gap to be as low as 10 or even five basis points by the end of the year.

Cyril Beuzit, bond analyst at Banque Nationale de Paris, said, however, he thought the French central bank would wait until the threat of social unrest in France had blown over before narrowing the gap.
